# The smaller-positive envelope by a negative-coordinate ratio extremum

**Theorem.** For m>=1 and 0<x_j<h<1, put

    rho=product_j(1-x_j), E=1/rho-1,
    B=sum_j x_j/(1-x_j), C=B/(1-rho)-1,
    Q=product_j(1+x_j/E), W=(1-h)C Q,
    R=rho(E+h)[1-(E+h)product_j(h-x_j)/h^(m+1)].

Then W>R. The nonstrict inequality holds on 0<=x_j<=h<1 if some x_j>0. This is the exact omitted-smaller-positive section-variance envelope. It is not a mixed-integer centerpoint theorem.

The proof uses two already proved inputs, with their precise scopes:

* The larger-positive scalar theorem in `candidate 31dd328861ee872c`: L=(1-sum x_j/E)Q>R in the open domain. Only one small-coordinate boundary limit below uses it.
* The exponential cap moment theorem in `candidate 16db32a020dc6379`, Section 1: for a homogeneous exponential cap of probability P, the product of the conditional means after omitting a positive-coefficient variable is at least P. This supplies upper-coordinate boundary values, as shown next.

All remaining steps are elementary differentiation, compactness, and strict convexity of one real function.

## 1. Signs, deletion, and upper-coordinate boundary

One has C>0: product_j(1-x_j)>=1-sum_j x_j implies 1-rho<=sum_j x_j<B whenever some x_j>0. Also Q>0. Thus W>0 for h<1 and nonzero x. In the interior 0<R: write p=1, q=1-h, and r_j=q x_j/(h-x_j)>0. For independent unit exponentials and V=pY_p+qY_q-sum r_jY_j, the exact exponential formulas give

    F=Pr(V>=0)=(E+h)product_j(h-x_j)/h^(m+1),
    X=product_j p/(p+r_j)>0,
    product_(i!=q) E(Y_i | V=0)=(X/h)W,
    F(1-F)=(X/h)R.                               (1)

Here conditional means at V=0 are the usual positive coarea ratios. In particular 0<F<1. Deleting x_j=0 leaves W and R unchanged, including their denominator powers.

At x_m=h, keep all other x_j<h and send the corresponding r_m to infinity, keeping p,q and the other coefficients fixed. Put V_0=pY_p+qY_q-sum_(j<m)r_jY_j, P=Pr(V_0>0), and M=E(V_0|V_0>0)>0. Conditioning on V_0 and dominated convergence give

    r_m F -> PM,
    E(Y_i|V=0) -> nu_i=E(Y_i|V_0>0), i!=m,
    r_m E(Y_m|V=0) -> M.

Therefore r_m times the difference in (1) tends to

    M[product_(i!=q,m)nu_i-P]>=0.

The inequality is precisely the cited exponential-cap moment theorem, selecting positive variable q. Since r_m X/h has a strictly positive finite limit, W>=R follows at this upper-coordinate face. Multiple coordinates equal to h follow by scalar continuity, because h<1 and E>0. No interior variance assertion is used to establish this boundary.

For m=1 direct factorization gives

    W-R=x(h-x)(1-h)(2h+x-hx)/[h^2(1-x)]>0.         (2)

This also gives the nonstrict boundary assertion for m=1.

## 2. Fixed-product reduction of a ratio maximum

Use induction on m for the nonstrict conclusion; m=1 is (2). Suppose it fails in dimension m>=2. Fix the E,h of any counterexample and maximize R/W on the compact set

    0<=x_j<=h, product_j(1-x_j)=1/(E+1).

This set excludes the all-zero vector, and W is strictly positive throughout, so the maximum exists. Its value exceeds one. By Section 1 and the induction hypothesis it cannot have an upper-coordinate or zero-coordinate boundary. It is therefore interior.

Keep all but two coordinates fixed and put u=1-x_i, v=1-x_j, uv=q_0, T=u+v. This preserves E. Along this motion B=B_o+T/q_0-2 and

    (E+x_i)(E+x_j)=(E+1)^2-(E+1)T+q_0.

Consequently W is a strictly concave quadratic in T: it is a positive constant times a positive-slope affine factor times a negative-slope affine factor. R is affine in T, since

    (h-x_i)(h-x_j)=(h-1)^2+(h-1)T+q_0.

If the maximal ratio is Lambda>1, Lambda W-R has a local minimum zero. It is strictly concave in T. When x_i!=x_j, T varies through an open interval while all coordinates remain interior, a contradiction. Thus every coordinate at this fixed-E,h ratio maximum is equal.

In particular every ratio value greater than one is bounded above by an equal-coordinate ratio value in the same dimension. This reduction preserves the actual threshold and the product defining E; it does not assert arbitrary smoothing decreases the gap.

## 3. All equal-coordinate boundary limits

For this section write x_j=x, 0<x<h<1, and

    E=(1-x)^(-m)-1, rho=(1-x)^m,
    M=C(1+x/E)^m, W=(1-h)M,
    L=(1-mx/E)(1+x/E)^m.

Every boundary sequence has limsup R/W<=1. Here are all possibilities.

If x tends to x_0 in (0,1) and h tends to x_0, Section 1 and continuity apply. If instead h tends to 1, differentiation of the exact R formula gives

    lim_(h->1) R/(1-h)=B-1+rho=(1-rho)C,
    lim_(h->1) R/W=(1-rho)/(1+x/E)^m<1.           (3)

Suppose x->0. The Taylor expansions, for fixed m, are

    E=mx+m(m+1)x^2/2+O(x^3),
    C=(m+1)x/2+O(x^2),
    1-mx/E=(m+1)x/2+O(x^2).

If also h->0, then W/L->1, and the already proved larger-positive inequality R<L implies limsup R/W<=1.

If h stays bounded away from zero, R/(1-h)=O(x^2) uniformly, while M/x tends to the strictly positive constant (m+1)(1+1/m)^m/2. To justify the uniform assertion, the displayed formula for R is analytic for |x| sufficiently small and h in a fixed [epsilon,1]. It vanishes identically at h=1, so division by 1-h has an analytic extension there. Moreover R(0,h)=partial_x R(0,h)=0 identically, as follows by differentiating rho and E at zero. The same identities hold after the removable division; a bounded second x derivative on this compact rectangle proves O(x^2). Therefore R/W->0.

Finally suppose x->1; then h->1. Put epsilon=1-x, delta=1-h, t=delta/epsilon in (0,1). An exact rearrangement is

    R=1-epsilon^m delta
      -(1-epsilon^m delta)^2(1-t)^m/(1-delta)^(m+1).

Since (1-delta)^(m+1)<=1 and (1-z)^2>=1-2z,

    R<=1-(1-2epsilon^m delta)(1-t)^m
      <=m t+2epsilon^(m+1)t.

Here the last step uses 1-(1-t)^m<=mt. Also Q>=1 and

    C=m(1-epsilon)/[epsilon(1-epsilon^m)]-1
      >=m/epsilon-(m+1).

For small epsilon the right side is positive, so

    W>=t[m-(m+1)epsilon],
    R/W<=[m+2epsilon^(m+1)]/[m-(m+1)epsilon] ->1.  (4)

This estimate is uniform even when t tends to zero. Equations (3)--(4) and the preceding cases exhaust the compact triangle 0<=x<=h<=1.

It follows that if any ratio exceeds one, its equal-coordinate supremum is finite and attained at 0<x<h<1. By Section 2 and induction, that attained point is also a global ratio maximum over all m-coordinate vectors. Thus it is legitimate to use arbitrary small common-coordinate and pair-product variations there. This is the only maximum-existence step in the argument, and every escaping boundary has been checked.

## 4. The exact negative-coordinate transformation

To analyze that hypothetical interior maximum, transform the original variables, here temporarily called X_j,H, by

    x_j=-X_j/(1-X_j), h=-H/(1-H).

The new domain is h<x_j<0. Define, in these new variables,

    rho=product_j(1-x_j), E=1/rho-1,
    L=(1-sum_j x_j/E)product_j(1+x_j/E),
    R=rho(E+h)[1-(E+h)product_j(h-x_j)/h^(m+1)].

Use rho_+,W_+,R_+ for the original positive-coordinate quantities. Direct substitution gives

    E=rho_+-1 in (-1,0),
    L=-C_+ Q_+/rho_+, R=-R_+/[rho_+(1-H)],
    R/L=R_+/W_+.                                (5)

In particular L<0 and R<0, and the transformation is a smooth bijection of the two open domains. The transformed F=(E+h)product(h-x_j)/h^(m+1) equals the same actual cap fraction as before, so 0<F<1. Thus a positive interior maximum of the original ratio becomes a positive interior maximum of R/L.

For fixed E,h the pair formula now is

    L(T)=C_*(E-S_o-2+T)[(E+1)^2-(E+1)T+q_0],
    C_*=product_(l!=i,j)(E+x_l)/E^(m+1)<0.

Hence L_TT=-2C_*(E+1)>0. At a ratio maximum Lambda>0, the function R-Lambda L has a local minimum zero (because L<0). Since R is affine, it is strictly concave in T. The equal-coordinate conclusion is consistent with Section 2. We will use the one-sided pair stability at that equal point, rather than an unjustified negative-domain location theorem.

## 5. Stationarity contradicts feasible pair stability

Write all transformed coordinates as x<0. Then

    E=(1-x)^(-m)-1 in (-1,0), U=E-mx>0,
    E'=m(E+1)/(1-x),
    Z=E((m+1)x-1)+mx=(1-x)(xE'-E)>0,
    A=(E+x)^2-(E+1)U=Z+x(E+x)>0,
    D=x[mh+(m+1)E]-Eh.

The assertions U>0 and Z>0 follow from strict convexity of E(x), with E(0)=0 and E'(0)=m. Also E+x<0.

Write F=(E+h)(h-x)^m/h^(m+1). The h derivative of R vanishes at a ratio maximum, since L is independent of h. Exact differentiation gives

    F/(1-F)=h(h-x)/D, D>0.                       (6)

Logarithms of -L and -R are legitimate. At a point satisfying (6), differentiation along the common-x variation gives

    L_x/L=m(m+1)xZ/[(1-x)E U(E+x)],
    R_x/R=m(m+1)x(1-h)/[(1-x)D].                 (7)

Both quantities are strictly negative. Ratio stationarity equates them, so

    E U(E+x)(1-h)=D Z.                           (8)

Solving this linear equation for h gives

    h=H_val=[E U(E+x)-(m+1)ExZ]/[(E+1)U^2].      (9)

Now split two equal coordinates while preserving their product, using u=(1-x)exp(s), v=(1-x)exp(-s). This permits T to increase from 2(1-x) and stays in the open domain for small s. The local minimum of R-Lambda L requires R_T-Lambda L_T>=0. Dividing by R=Lambda L<0 reverses the sign, yielding

    L_T/L>=R_T/R.

The exact pair derivatives are

    L_T/L=A/[U(E+x)^2],
    R_T/R=h(1-h)/[(h-x)D].                      (10)

Substitute (8) into (10). All denominator signs are fixed: U>0, (E+x)^2>0, and E(h-x)>0. Thus

    E(h-x)A-h(E+x)Z>=0.

Its exact factorization is

    x{h(E+1)U-EA}.

Since x<0, the necessary pair-stability bound is

    h<=H_b:=EA/[(E+1)U].                        (11)

But exact subtraction in (9)--(11) gives

    H_val-H_b
      =E(E+x)(1-x)[2E-x(E'+m)]/[(E+1)U^2].      (12)

Every factor outside the square bracket is strictly positive. The derivative E'(s)=m(1-s)^(-m-1) is strictly convex on [x,0]. Its integral mean is strictly below the average of its endpoint values:

    E(x)/x=(1/(-x)) integral_x^0 E'(s) ds
      <[E'(x)+E'(0)]/2=(E'+m)/2.

Multiplication by x<0 gives 2E>x(E'+m). Thus (12) is strictly positive, contradicting h=H_val and h<=H_b.

There is no positive interior ratio maximum of the kind supplied by Section 3. The supposed ratio greater than one is impossible, completing induction and proving W>=R.

If equality held at any open-domain point with m>=2, the now proved global bound would make it a positive local ratio maximum. The fixed-product argument again forces equal coordinates, and the same strict contradiction applies. Combined with (2), this proves W>R throughout the open domain.

## 6. Simplex consequence and exact scope

Let a d-simplex, d>=2, have a proper hyperplane section with exactly two positive vertex heights p>q>0, any number of zero heights, and at least one negative height. Let F be the captured volume fraction and b the actual section barycentric centroid. The exponential section identities and zero-phase treatment in `candidate fdab4307532951f8` give

    d^d product_(i!=q)b_i-F(1-F)=(X/h)(W-R)>0.

Together with the larger-positive theorem, this proves the strict section-variance bound with EITHER positive vertex omitted whenever the two positive heights differ. Equal positive heights follow by the fully justified coarea continuity argument in that source; for that case only the nonstrict conclusion is asserted here. Zero heights have section exponential mean exactly one, so original dimension d and its exact d^d factor are preserved.

No bound with a negative vertex omitted, no all-coordinate product bound, and no global mixed-integer conclusion is inferred from this theorem.
